(Entertainment Weekly) -- After all the anticipation and hubbub, the weekend is coming to an end and the box office results are here: "Watchmen" (No. 1) grossed $55.7 million during its first frame, according to early estimates from Media by Numbers. "Watchmen" led the weekend box office, grossing $55.7 million during its first weekend. That's a solid sum, to be sure, although it's certainly on the low end of most projections. "Watchmen" premiered in more theaters (3,611) than any other R-rated movie in history, and it averaged an impressive $15,413 per venue, despite a potentially problematic long running time. It also scored the biggest debut of 2009 so far. Nonetheless, the movie's $55.7 million take (including $5.5 million from 124 IMAX screens) is substantially smaller than the $70.9 million that 300, the last R-rated graphic-novel movie from director Zack Snyder, earned on its opening weekend two years ago. And aside from that theater-count statistic (which almost any film could break at any time, really), there will be no major records to report on this weekend (for example, "Watchmen's" debut was just the fifth-best opening ever for an R-rated movie). I'd argue, in fact, that this opening is a bit soft, considering the great expectations that came with Snyder's adaptation of Alan Moore's landmark comic book -- not to mention "Watchmen's" hefty grosses from screenings at midnight on Friday and throughout its first day. After attracting some major initial interest, banking $25.1 million on Friday, the film's audience dropped off dramatically during the weekend: It grossed $19 million on Saturday and is expected to bring in just $11.5 million on Sunday. These are all big numbers, don't get me wrong, but, when combined with the fact that the film got a lukewarm CinemaScore grade of B from an audience that was largely comprised of older men, it all points to a rapid downward trend that may be difficult to reverse in the weeks to come. Elsewhere -- yes, there were other movies playing at the multiplex this weekend! -- a number of films continued to do what "Watchmen" must now aspire to, perhaps in vain: They stayed strong deep into their long runs. Tyler Perry's "Madea Goes to Jail" (No. 2) grossed $8.8 million on its third weekend; the film, Perry's biggest yet at the box office, has banked $76.5 million to date. "Taken" (No. 3) also moved along like the unstoppable force it has been for more than a month now, earning $7.5 million and bringing its six-week sum to $118 million. Best Picture winner "Slumdog Millionaire" (No. 4) was next with $6.9 million, which boosted its domestic haul to $125.4 million. And "Paul Blart: Mall Cop" (No. 5) took its eight-week total to $133.6 million thanks to another $4.2 million gross. iReport.com: What did you think of 'Watchmen'? Meanwhile, "Jonas Brothers: The 3D Concert Experience" (No. 9) completely fell off the map, dropping a staggering 78 percent to gross just $2.8 million. According to Box Office Mojo, that's the 15th biggest second-weekend decline of all time. Overall, the cumulative box office was up nearly 8 percent over the same frame a year ago, when 10,000 B.C. opened big, making this the fifth consecutive "up" weekend at the multiplex. (Entertainment Weekly) — After weeks of anticipation and considerable buzz, the weekend is drawing to a close, and the box office results are in: “Watchmen” debuted at No. 1 with $55.7 million in its first frame, according to early estimates from Media by Numbers.

“Watchmen” led the weekend box office, grossing $55.7 million during its opening weekend. That is certainly a solid figure, though it falls on the lower end of most projections. The film opened in more theaters—3,611—than any other R-rated movie in history and averaged an impressive $15,413 per venue, despite its potentially challenging lengthy running time. It also delivered the biggest debut of 2009 so far.

Even so, the movie’s $55.7 million haul, which includes $5.5 million from 124 IMAX screens, is substantially below the $70.9 million earned on opening weekend by “300,” director Zack Snyder’s previous R-rated graphic-novel adaptation, two years ago. And apart from the theater-count milestone—which, in truth, almost any film could surpass at any time—there are no major records to report this weekend. For example, “Watchmen” posted only the fifth-best opening ever for an R-rated film.

In fact, I would argue that this opening is somewhat soft, given the enormous expectations surrounding Snyder’s adaptation of Alan Moore’s landmark comic book—not to mention the film’s strong grosses from midnight screenings on Friday and throughout its first day. After drawing significant initial interest and taking in $25.1 million on Friday, the film’s audience declined sharply over the rest of the weekend: it grossed $19 million on Saturday and is expected to earn just $11.5 million on Sunday.

These are still substantial numbers, to be clear. But when combined with the film’s lukewarm CinemaScore grade of B from an audience composed largely of older men, they suggest a rapid downward trend that may prove difficult to reverse in the weeks ahead.

Elsewhere—yes, there were other movies playing at the multiplex this weekend—a number of films continued to do what “Watchmen” must now hope to achieve, perhaps in vain: remain strong well into their theatrical runs.

Tyler Perry’s “Madea Goes to Jail” ranked No. 2, grossing $8.8 million in its third weekend. The film, Perry’s biggest box-office success to date, has earned $76.5 million so far. “Taken” came in at No. 3 and continued its remarkably steady run, earning $7.5 million and bringing its six-week total to $118 million. Best Picture winner “Slumdog Millionaire” followed at No. 4 with $6.9 million, lifting its domestic total to $125.4 million. “Paul Blart: Mall Cop” rounded out the top five, adding $4.2 million and raising its eight-week total to $133.6 million.

iReport.com: What did you think of “Watchmen”?

Meanwhile, “Jonas Brothers: The 3D Concert Experience” fell sharply at No. 9, plunging a staggering 78 percent to gross just $2.8 million. According to Box Office Mojo, that ranks as the 15th-largest second-weekend decline of all time.

Overall, the cumulative box office was up nearly 8 percent compared with the same frame a year ago, when “10,000 B.C.” opened strongly, making this the fifth consecutive “up” weekend at the multiplex. All in all, I would say today’s report was a good one indeed.

That total is certainly respectable, but it falls toward the lower end of many expectations. It also delivered the biggest opening weekend of 2009 up to that point.

Its opening, for instance, ranks only fifth among R-rated debuts.

In fact, given the enormous expectations surrounding Snyder’s version of Alan Moore’s celebrated comic book, as well as the strong grosses from midnight Friday showings and throughout opening day, the start seems somewhat underwhelming. After drawing intense early interest and earning $25.1 million on Friday, the film saw attendance fall sharply as the weekend went on. It made $19 million on Saturday and was projected to collect only $11.5 million on Sunday.

Those are still large figures, certainly. But when paired with the movie’s modest CinemaScore grade of B from an audience made up largely of older men, they suggest a steep decline that could be hard to stop in the coming weeks.

Elsewhere — because, yes, other movies were also playing at theaters this weekend — several titles continued doing what “Watchmen” now needs to do, though perhaps may struggle to achieve: hold up well far into their runs.

Tyler Perry’s “Madea Goes to Jail” landed in second place with $8.8 million in its third weekend. The movie, Perry’s highest-grossing release so far, has earned $76.5 million to date. “Taken,” in third place, continued its strong run after more than a month in theaters, adding $7.5 million for a six-week total of $118 million. Best Picture winner “Slumdog Millionaire” followed in fourth with $6.9 million, lifting its domestic total to $125.4 million. In fifth place, “Paul Blart: Mall Cop” earned another $4.2 million, bringing its eight-week total to $133.6 million.

*March 9, 2009*

Zack Snyder’s long-awaited superhero epic **“Watchmen”** stormed into theaters this weekend with an estimated **$55.7 million** debut, easily taking the No. 1 spot at the North American box office. But while the Warner Bros. release delivered one of the biggest openings ever for an R-rated film, its weekend trajectory suggested that the film may be playing more strongly to devoted fans than to general audiences.

The adaptation of Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons’ landmark graphic novel opened huge on Friday, grossing about **$24.5 million**, including midnight screenings. By Saturday, however, business fell noticeably, and Sunday estimates pointed to a steep overall slide from opening day. The film’s **Friday-to-Sunday drop** has become the weekend’s major talking point, with industry watchers noting that fan-driven titles often burn brightest on opening day.

Audience reaction also appeared mixed. **“Watchmen” earned a B CinemaScore**, a respectable but not especially enthusiastic grade for a big-budget comic-book release. The film’s lengthy running time, dark tone and dense source material may have limited its appeal beyond the core fan base.

One clear bright spot was IMAX. Playing on **124 IMAX screens**, “Watchmen” grossed approximately **$5.4 million** from the format, setting a strong pace and underscoring the value of premium-ticket presentations for event films.

Behind “Watchmen,” Tyler Perry’s **“Madea Goes to Jail”** continued to show staying power, placing second with roughly **$8.8 million** in its third weekend. The Lionsgate comedy has now pushed its domestic total past **$76 million**, making it one of Perry’s strongest performers to date.

Fox’s action hit **“Taken”** remained a durable crowd-pleaser, taking in about **$7.5 million** for third place. The Liam Neeson thriller has become one of the year’s early sleeper successes, climbing past **$118 million** domestically.

Fresh off its Academy Awards triumph, **“Slumdog Millionaire”** continued to benefit from Oscar momentum. The Best Picture winner earned around **$6.9 million**, bringing its North American total to approximately **$125 million**.

Rounding out the upper tier, Sony’s **“Paul Blart: Mall Cop”** added about **$4.2 million**, continuing its remarkably strong run. The Kevin James comedy has now grossed more than **$133 million**, making it one of the surprise comedy hits of the season.

counterfactuals.output:
## Was *Watchmen*’s Weekend Win Really a Disappointment?

*Watchmen* didn’t just win the weekend — it dominated it. Zack Snyder’s long-awaited adaptation of Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons’ famously “unfilmable” graphic novel opened at No. 1 with an estimated **$55 million** at the domestic box office, easily outpacing the rest of the marketplace.

So why did the victory lap feel a little muted?

Because for a movie like *Watchmen*, context is everything. This wasn’t a quiet March genre release that surprised the industry. It was a heavily marketed, fanboy-anointed event film from the director of *300*, arriving with years of anticipation, wall-to-wall publicity, and a built-in audience that had been waiting decades to see Rorschach, Dr. Manhattan, and Nite Owl on the big screen.

A $55 million debut is, by almost any normal standard, a strong opening — especially for an **R-rated**, nearly **three-hour**, densely plotted superhero deconstruction with more Cold War dread and existential angst than crowd-pleasing quips. But *Watchmen* wasn’t being measured against normal standards. It was being measured against expectations.

And that’s where things get complicated.

Going into the weekend, some observers expected *Watchmen* to open closer to the blockbuster tier — perhaps not *The Dark Knight* territory, but certainly higher than a mid-$50 million start. Snyder’s *300* opened to about **$70 million** two years earlier, also in March, also with an R rating, also based on a graphic novel. That comparison was always a little unfair: *300* was simpler, shorter, more visceral, and far easier to sell in a trailer. *Watchmen*, by contrast, is a morally thorny alternate-history epic whose most famous character walks around glowing blue and debating the nature of humanity.

Still, studios don’t spend big money on “unfair” comparisons by accident. The marketing campaign sold *Watchmen* as a major cultural event, and the fan base turned out early. The question is whether anyone else did.

That’s the real concern. The film’s audience appeared heavily front-loaded, driven by comic devotees and Snyder fans eager to show up on opening night. Its Friday-to-Sunday pattern suggested intense initial demand but not necessarily broad mainstream momentum. And with mixed word of mouth — some viewers calling it bold and faithful, others finding it cold, long, or simply weird — *Watchmen* faced the possibility of a steep second-weekend drop.

In other words: winning the weekend was never the issue. Legs were.

For Warner Bros., the math was not disastrous, but it wasn’t automatically triumphant either. With a sizable production budget and a major marketing spend, *Watchmen* needed more than a flashy opening weekend. It needed staying power, international strength, and a healthy afterlife on DVD and Blu-ray — where the property’s devoted fan base would likely remain valuable.

The film’s performance also underlined a lesson Hollywood relearns every few years: not all comic-book properties are created equal. By 2009, the superhero genre was booming, but *Watchmen* was never a conventional superhero movie. It was a critique of superhero mythology, not an uncomplicated celebration of it. That distinction may thrill readers of the graphic novel, but it can be a tougher sell to casual moviegoers expecting escapism.

So was *Watchmen*’s opening disappointing?

The answer is: **only relative to the hype**.

A $55 million March debut for a dark, R-rated, adult-skewing comic adaptation is objectively impressive. But for a film positioned as the next great comic-book movie event, the opening fell short of the most bullish expectations. *Watchmen* won the box office battle decisively — but the weekend also suggested that its appeal might be narrower than its marketing campaign implied.

In true *Watchmen* fashion, the verdict is morally gray: a hit on paper, a question mark in practice.

## Movie Industry Report: *Watchmen* Opening Weekend Performance  
**Date:** March 2009  
**Subject:** Warner Bros.’ R-rated superhero epic opens strongly, but early indicators point to front-loaded box office trajectory.

### Executive Summary

Warner Bros.’ *Watchmen* opened in first place at the domestic box office over the March 6–8, 2009 weekend, grossing an estimated **$55.2 million** from **3,611 theaters**. The debut represents one of the strongest March openings on record and sets a new benchmark for the **widest release ever for an R-rated film** at the time.

However, despite the impressive launch, *Watchmen* fell short of the opening weekend of director Zack Snyder’s previous comic-book adaptation, *300*, which debuted to approximately **$70.9 million** in March 2007. Early weekend patterns suggest *Watchmen* may be significantly more front-loaded than *300*, raising questions about its long-term domestic box office prospects.

---

## Opening Weekend Performance

*Watchmen* entered the marketplace with major awareness, driven by a long-running marketing campaign, strong fan anticipation, and the reputation of Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons’ graphic novel as one of the most acclaimed works in comic-book history.

The film opened with:

- **Domestic weekend gross:** Approximately **$55.2 million**
- **Theater count:** **3,611 locations**
- **Per-theater average:** Roughly **$15,000+**
- **Distributor:** Warner Bros.
- **Rating:** R
- **Director:** Zack Snyder

The opening is undeniably strong for an R-rated, nearly three-hour superhero film with dense source material and a darker tone than mainstream comic-book fare. It confirms that the *Watchmen* brand, while not as broadly familiar as Batman, Spider-Man, or Superman, had enough cultural weight and marketing support to generate a major opening weekend.

---

## Record Theater Count for an R-Rated Film

One of the weekend’s key industry milestones was *Watchmen*’s theater count. Opening in **3,611 theaters**, the film became the **widest R-rated release in history** at the time.

This reflects Warner Bros.’ confidence in the property and its desire to position *Watchmen* not as a niche comic-book adaptation, but as a major event film. The release strategy mirrored that of a summer tentpole despite the March date and adult rating.

The record-wide rollout also helped maximize demand among core fans immediately, though it may contribute to steeper declines in subsequent weekends if casual audiences do not expand the film’s reach.

---

## Comparison to Zack Snyder’s *300*

The most immediate comparison is Snyder’s previous Warner Bros. release, *300*, which opened in March 2007 and became a breakout hit.

### Opening Weekend Comparison

| Film | Opening Weekend | Theaters | Rating | Domestic Total |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|
| *300* | ~$70.9 million | ~3,103 | R | ~$210.6 million |
| *Watchmen* | ~$55.2 million | 3,611 | R | TBD |

While *Watchmen* had a wider release, it opened about **$15 million below *300***. That is notable because *300* had fewer pre-existing barriers for mainstream audiences: it was shorter, more action-driven, visually straightforward, and easier to market as a high-energy war spectacle.

By contrast, *Watchmen* is more challenging commercially. It is a revisionist superhero drama with a sprawling ensemble, moral ambiguity, political themes, and a runtime of approximately **2 hours and 40 minutes**. These factors make it less accessible to general audiences and reduce daily showtime capacity.

---

## Signs of Front-Loading

The opening weekend suggests *Watchmen* benefited heavily from fan-driven demand. Midnight and Friday grosses were especially strong, indicating that the core audience turned out immediately.

That pattern is common for high-profile genre films, particularly adaptations with built-in fan bases. The concern is whether the film can move beyond that audience in the weeks ahead.

Factors pointing to potentially limited legs include:

1. **Hard R rating**  
   The adult rating limits younger attendance and family viewing.

2. **Long runtime**  
   At nearly three hours, theaters can schedule fewer showings per day, limiting capacity and repeat viewing potential.

3. **Mixed mainstream response**  
   While many fans and critics appreciated the ambition and fidelity to the graphic novel, general audience reaction appears more divided.

4. **Dense subject matter**  
   The film is less of a conventional superhero action movie than marketing may have suggested.

5. **Large initial theater count**  
   A very wide opening can burn off demand quickly, leading to steeper second-weekend drops.

---

## Implications for Future Box Office Legs

The central question is whether *Watchmen* can follow the model of *300*, which held well enough to reach over **$200 million domestic**, or whether it will perform more like a fan-driven event film with a sharp second-weekend decline.

At this stage, *300*-level legs appear unlikely. To match *300*’s domestic total, *Watchmen* would need a multiplier of nearly four times its opening weekend, which is improbable given its front-loaded opening pattern and more polarizing content.

A more realistic domestic outcome may depend on how steeply it falls in weekend two. If the film drops in the range of 55% to 60%, it could still stabilize and finish respectably. If the decline is closer to 65% or more, it would indicate that the film’s appeal is concentrated primarily among devoted fans.

Given the opening weekend data, a domestic finish in the **$120 million to $150 million range** appears more plausible than a run approaching *300*’s $210 million.

---

## Industry Takeaway

*Watchmen*’s opening weekend demonstrates that adult-oriented comic-book properties can still generate blockbuster-level launches when backed by strong marketing and fan enthusiasm. Its record R-rated theater count underscores the industry’s growing willingness to treat mature graphic novel adaptations as major studio releases.

However, the film’s future box office will depend less on awareness and more on audience satisfaction. Unlike *300*, which translated its style and simplicity into broad appeal, *Watchmen* is more complex, longer, darker, and less conventionally crowd-pleasing.

The opening is a success, but the weekend numbers also suggest a film that may have already captured much of its most motivated audience. For Warner Bros., the challenge now is whether *Watchmen* can expand beyond the faithful—or whether its box office will prove as front-loaded as many fan-driven genre releases.
